common_name: Double Zahara Fire Zinnia (AAS-Winning Fully Double Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; Double Zahara Fire, a 2010 AAS winner alongside Double Zahara Cherry, brought fully double flowers in a bright fire-orange to the Zahara series.

directions: Sow seed a quarter-inch deep in full sun after the last frost has passed, or set out transplants once nights stay warm. Double Zahara Fire carries the same vivid orange-red color as the single-flowered Zahara Fire, but each bloom opens fully double with layers of ruffled petals packed into a dense, rounded flower head. Like its AAS-winning series mate Double Zahara Cherry, it keeps the Zahara line's dense, self-cleaning growth habit, dropping spent flowers cleanly so no deadheading is needed through a long summer bloom season. Expect the same strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot that lets Zahara selections shrug off humid, wet conditions that damage older bedding zinnias.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Zahara Coral Rose Zinnia (AAS-Winning Coral-Pink Landscape Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; Zahara Coral Rose was a 2010 AAS winner and remains one of the most widely grown colors in the Zahara series.

directions: Sow seed a quarter-inch deep after the last frost, or transplant seedlings into full sun with room to branch. Zahara Coral Rose bears single, warm coral-pink flowers about two and a half inches across on a dense, well-branched mound, one of the original AAS-winning colors that established the Zahara series' reputation for disease resistance. Like its series mates Zahara Sunburst and Zahara White, it blooms continuously without deadheading, dropping spent flowers cleanly as new buds open. The plants tolerate heat, humidity, and drought with ease, standing up to the powdery mildew and leaf spot pressure that damages standard garden zinnias through a Gulf Coast summer.

common_name: Zahara White Zinnia (AAS-Winning White Landscape Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; Zahara White earned a 2006 AAS Award, the first color recognized in what became the broader Zahara series.

directions: Sow seed a quarter-inch deep in full sun after the last frost, or set out transplants once the soil has warmed. Zahara White opens clean, pure white single flowers around two and a half inches across on a compact, mounding plant, the earliest AAS-winning color in the Zahara line that later added Coral Rose and Sunburst. It shares the series' self-cleaning habit, continuously producing new buds through summer without deadheading, and its pale color makes it a useful brightener for mixed beds and evening gardens. Strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot keeps foliage clean even through the hot, humid conditions that plague older zinnia varieties.

common_name: Potomac Appleblossom Snapdragon (Tall Single-Stem Greenhouse Cut-Flower Snapdragon)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. Potomac Appleblossom is grown as a single-stem crop under the cool temperatures of fall, winter, or early spring production and is often netted or strung for straight, unbranched stems.

directions: Start seed indoors 12 to 16 weeks before transplanting, surface-sowing since the fine seed needs light to germinate. Potomac Appleblossom is the soft pink-and-white bicolor selection within the tall Potomac greenhouse snapdragon series, opening densely packed spurred florets along a single unbranched spike that reaches three to four feet under cool-season production. Like its series mates Potomac Rose and Potomac Yellow, it is grown as a netted, single-stem crop with no pinching, so all of the plant's energy channels into one dominant flower spike prized for its heavy stem strength and long vase life. Schedule it for fall-through-spring harvest in mild climates or heated structures, since snapdragons perform best under cool temperatures.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Potomac Ivory Snapdragon (Tall Single-Stem Greenhouse Cut-Flower Snapdragon)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. Potomac Ivory is grown as a single-stem crop under the cool temperatures of fall, winter, or early spring production and is often netted or strung for straight, unbranched stems.

directions: Sow seed indoors 12 to 16 weeks before transplanting, pressing it onto the surface of moist mix without covering, since light aids germination. Potomac Ivory produces soft creamy-white spikes within the tall Potomac series, a neutral shade that greenhouse growers use to round out mixed-color snapdragon bunches alongside Potomac Lavender and Potomac White. Support netting keeps the three-to-four-foot single stems straight for harvest, and growers avoid pinching so each plant commits its energy to one dominant, densely flowered spike. Cool fall, winter, or early spring production gives the strongest stems and the longest vase life.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Potomac Rose Snapdragon (Tall Single-Stem Greenhouse Cut-Flower Snapdragon)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. Potomac Rose is grown as a single-stem crop under the cool temperatures of fall, winter, or early spring production and is often netted or strung for straight, unbranched stems.

directions: Start seed indoors 12 to 16 weeks before the planned transplant date, surface-sowing since germination needs light. Potomac Rose bears rich rose-pink florets densely packed along a straight, unbranched spike, one of the deeper-colored selections in the tall Potomac greenhouse series alongside the paler Potomac Appleblossom. Growers net or string the plants and skip pinching so each one puts all its growth into a single three-to-four-foot stem valued for its stiffness and long vase life. Like the rest of the series it is scheduled for cool-season production, typically harvested from fall through spring in unheated or lightly heated structures.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Potomac White Snapdragon (Tall Single-Stem Greenhouse Cut-Flower Snapdragon)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. Potomac White is grown as a single-stem crop under the cool temperatures of fall, winter, or early spring production and is often netted or strung for straight, unbranched stems.

directions: Surface-sow seed indoors 12 to 16 weeks before transplanting, since Potomac snapdragon seed needs light to germinate reliably. Potomac White opens pure white florets tightly packed along a single tall, unbranched spike, a staple neutral color that cut-flower growers pair with Potomac Rose and Potomac Yellow for mixed bunches. As with the rest of the series, plants are grown netted and unpinched so all their energy goes into one straight, sturdy stem reaching three to four feet. Cool growing conditions through fall, winter, or early spring produce the stiffest stems and the best vase life.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Potomac Yellow Snapdragon (Tall Single-Stem Greenhouse Cut-Flower Snapdragon)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. Potomac Yellow is grown as a single-stem crop under the cool temperatures of fall, winter, or early spring production and is often netted or strung for straight, unbranched stems.

directions: Sow seed indoors 12 to 16 weeks before transplanting, surface-sowing without covering since the seed germinates best with light exposure. Potomac Yellow carries clear golden-yellow florets closely packed on a single tall, unbranched spike within the greenhouse-grade Potomac series, a bright complement to the softer Potomac Ivory and Potomac Appleblossom shades. Growers net the plants and avoid pinching so each one channels its growth into one dominant three-to-four-foot stem with the stiffness and vase life the series is known for. Fall-through-spring production under cool temperatures gives the strongest, straightest stems.

common_name: Potomac Lavender Snapdragon (Tall Single-Stem Greenhouse Cut-Flower Snapdragon)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. Potomac Lavender is grown as a single-stem crop under the cool temperatures of fall, winter, or early spring production and is often netted or strung for straight, unbranched stems.

directions: Start seed indoors 12 to 16 weeks ahead of transplanting, surface-sowing since germination is light-dependent. Potomac Lavender opens soft lavender-blue florets along a single dense spike, a cool-toned option in the tall Potomac series that pairs well with Potomac Rose and Potomac White in mixed cut-flower bunches. Like the rest of the series, plants are netted and left unpinched so growth concentrates into one straight, sturdy three-to-four-foot stem. Cool-season greenhouse or high-tunnel production from fall through spring produces the strongest stems and the longest vase life.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: ProCut Lemon Sunflower (Single-Stem Pale-Yellow Cut Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is above 60°F, repeating sowings every 1-2 weeks through midsummer for a steady supply of stems.

directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep on tight 6-9 inch spacing in full sun so each plant channels its growth into a single unbranched stem topped by one flower. ProCut Lemon is the palest yellow member of the industry-standard ProCut single-stem line, a soft, cool tone distinct from the deeper gold and orange shades elsewhere in the series. Because the flowers are pollen-free, they hold up cleanly in mixed bouquets without shedding pollen on fabric or other blooms. The whole planting matures and flowers together in a tight window around 55-65 days, so succession sow every one to two weeks through midsummer to keep cut stems coming.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: QIS Yellow Statice (Compact Branching Cut-Flower Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots, since statice resents root disturbance; transplant after hardening off into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. QIS Yellow is sold as a single-color selection within the QIS series alongside a blended mix.

directions: Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays, since statice seedlings resent root disturbance and transplant best while still young. QIS Yellow carries golden-yellow papery calyces on the same compact, well-branched habit that defines the QIS series, yielding an unusually heavy number of straight stems per plant for a statice of its size. Harden off and transplant into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, and cut stems for fresh bouquets or hang them upside down in a warm, dark space to dry, where the color holds for years. Its tolerance for salt and drought makes it as useful in coastal cutting gardens as in hot, dry inland sites.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: QIS Rose Statice (Compact Branching Cut-Flower Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots, since statice resents root disturbance; transplant after hardening off into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. QIS Rose is sold as a single-color selection within the QIS series alongside a blended mix.

directions: Sow seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, starting it in cell trays or small pots since statice does not transplant well once its roots are disturbed. QIS Rose bears warm rose-pink calyces on the same short, uniform, heavily branched plants shared across the QIS series, producing more straight cutting stems per plant than older open-pollinated statice strains. Move hardened-off transplants into full sun and well-drained soil after the last frost, and either use the papery flowers fresh or air-dry them upside down for long-lasting arrangements. Plants tolerate heat, drought, and salt spray, making them dependable in exposed coastal or dry inland cutting gardens.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: QIS Blue Statice (Compact Branching Cut-Flower Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots, since statice resents root disturbance; transplant after hardening off into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. QIS Blue is sold as a single-color selection within the QIS series alongside a blended mix.

directions: Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays, since statice transplants best while still young and resents having its roots disturbed later. QIS Blue produces true blue-violet papery calyces on the same compact, well-branched framework shared throughout the QIS series, a color prized by cut-flower growers for both fresh mixed bouquets and dried everlasting arrangements. Harden off seedlings and set them into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, and hang cut stems upside down in a warm, dark space to preserve their color for dried use. Like its series mates, it tolerates salt spray, heat, and drought with ease.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: QIS Purple Statice (Compact Branching Cut-Flower Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots, since statice resents root disturbance; transplant after hardening off into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. QIS Purple is sold as a single-color selection within the QIS series alongside a blended mix.

directions: Sow seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or small pots, since statice seedlings dislike having their roots disturbed once established. QIS Purple bears deep violet-purple calyces on the same short, uniform, densely branched plants found throughout the QIS series, giving growers a rich, saturated color for both fresh cutting and dried-flower work. Transplant hardened-off seedlings into full sun and well-drained soil after the last frost, and air-dry harvested stems upside down in a warm, dark location to hold their color for years. Plants shrug off heat, drought, and salty coastal conditions that limit many other cut-flower species.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: QIS White Statice (Compact Branching Cut-Flower Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots, since statice resents root disturbance; transplant after hardening off into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. QIS White is sold as a single-color selection within the QIS series alongside a blended mix.

directions: Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, sowing into cell trays since statice resents root disturbance during transplanting. QIS White opens clean white papery calyces on the same compact, heavily branched plants shared across the QIS series, a neutral color growers use to round out mixed cut-flower and dried-flower bunches. Harden off and move seedlings into full sun and well-drained soil after frost danger passes, and either cut stems fresh or hang them upside down to air-dry for long-lasting arrangements. The plants tolerate salt spray, heat, and drought better than most other cut-flower annuals.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: QIS Apricot Statice (Compact Branching Cut-Flower Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots, since statice resents root disturbance; transplant after hardening off into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. QIS Apricot is sold as a single-color selection within the QIS series alongside a blended mix.

directions: Sow seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays, since statice transplants poorly once its roots have become established in an open flat. QIS Apricot carries soft peachy-orange calyces on the same short, evenly branched plants common to the QIS series, a warm pastel shade that blends easily with the brighter yellows and pinks elsewhere in the line. Harden off seedlings and transplant into full sun and well-drained soil once frost has passed, then cut for fresh arrangements or air-dry stems upside down to preserve the color indefinitely. Like its series mates, it holds up well to heat, drought, and salty coastal air.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: QIS Carmine Rose Statice (Compact Branching Cut-Flower Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots, since statice resents root disturbance; transplant after hardening off into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. QIS Carmine Rose is sold as a single-color selection within the QIS series alongside a blended mix.

directions: Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or small pots, since statice seedlings resent later root disturbance. QIS Carmine Rose bears deep carmine-pink calyces, one of the more saturated colors in the QIS series, on the same compact, well-branched habit bred for heavy stem counts per plant. Transplant hardened-off seedlings into full sun and well-drained soil after the last frost, and either use stems fresh in bouquets or hang them upside down to air-dry, where the vivid color holds for years. Salt, heat, and drought tolerance make it as reliable in coastal gardens as in hot, dry inland sites.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Sunstar Red II Pentas (Large-Flowered Proven Winners Star-Cluster Pentas)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants after the last frost once nights stay warm; Sunstar Red II is the deep true-red color in the large-flowered Sunstar pentas series.

directions: Sunstar Red II opens dense, oversized clusters of true-red star-shaped florets, one of the boldest colors in the large-flowered Sunstar series alongside its series mates Sunstar Pink and Sunstar Rose. Plant it in full sun and consistently moist, well-drained soil, where the heavy flower domes draw steady hummingbird and butterfly traffic from summer into fall. Because it runs larger and wider than seed-grown pentas types, give it extra room in beds and containers so neighboring plants are not crowded as the flower heads expand. No deadheading is needed; light, regular fertilizing through the season supports the heavier bloom load this series is bred to carry.

common_name: Sunstar Pink Pentas (Large-Flowered Proven Winners Star-Cluster Pentas)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants after the last frost once nights stay warm; Sunstar Pink is the clear pink color in the large-flowered Sunstar pentas series.

directions: Sunstar Pink bears large, dense clusters of clear pink star-shaped florets on the same oversized flower heads that distinguish the Sunstar series from seed-grown pentas types. Set plants in full sun with consistently moist, well-drained soil, where the heavy blooms pull in pollinators and hummingbirds from summer through fall without any deadheading. Give it generous spacing compared to smaller pentas cultivars, since Sunstar plants and their flower domes both run larger than average. Steady light feeding through the growing season keeps the extra-large clusters coming alongside series mates Sunstar Red II and Sunstar Rose.

common_name: Sunstar Rose Pentas (Large-Flowered Proven Winners Star-Cluster Pentas)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants after the last frost once nights stay warm; Sunstar Rose is the deeper rosy-pink color in the large-flowered Sunstar pentas series.

directions: Sunstar Rose carries rich rosy-pink star-shaped florets in the same oversized, dense clusters bred into the whole Sunstar series, a deeper tone than its series mate Sunstar Pink. Grow it in full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil, where the large flower heads draw heavy pollinator and hummingbird activity all summer into fall. Because Sunstar plants size up larger and wider than seed-grown pentas, space them generously in beds and containers so the flower domes can fully expand. Regular light fertilizing supports the heavier bloom load the series is known for, and no deadheading is required to keep it flowering continuously.

common_name: You and Me Expression Hydrangea (Reblooming Bigleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Expression carries the same reblooming habit as its You and Me series siblings Together and Romance, flowering on both old and new wood.

directions: Expression rounds out the You and Me series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas bred by Michael Dirr and marketed by Bailey Nurseries alongside siblings Together, Romance, and Forever, distinguished within the group by its own combination of flower form and color. Like the rest of the series, it sets buds on both old and new wood, so a hard winter or an aggressive pruning still leaves plants able to produce a solid late-summer rebloom. Plant it in evenly moist, humus-rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and mulch to buffer root-zone temperature swings that cause wilting in large-leaved reblooming mopheads. Limit pruning to spent blooms and dead wood so the earliest old-wood flush is not sacrificed.
sources: Bailey Nurseries — You and Me Hydrangea Series
